voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
To us Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary – both, in the same breath, confessed by every household under our catechism each week. He is our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the only one who stands between us and God on our behalf – no saint, no teacher, no priest of ours beside him. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Every page of Scripture points to him. We say it this way, in the catechism's own voice, in each believer's mouth: "He is my Lord! I am His very own".

Here is the Second Article as our households said it:

And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary; suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried. He descended into Hell; on the third day rose again from death; ascended into Heaven; He is seated at the right hand of God, the Father Almighty; from where He will come to judge the living and the dead.

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
He redeemed us – a lost and condemned people – and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. He died to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins. On the third day he rose again from death, and we confess that as he is risen from death, he lives and reigns forever. That is what he did, and that is what we confess, each week, in every household.

Here is how the catechism teaches it, in the Second Article's own explanation:

I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary; that He is my Lord! I am His very own -- who has redeemed me, a lost and condemned person, bought back and won me from all sins, from death, and from the power of the devil: not with gold or silver, but with His holy, precious blood, His innocent body -- His death! So that I should be His very own, live under Him in His kingdom, and serve Him in everlasting righteousness, innocence, and salvation; just as He is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
Justification is God's act of naming a sinner righteous. In the same breath, God also makes that sinner righteous. Both happen through faith, for Christ's sake alone. This is the center of our whole teaching.

Faith itself is trust that holds onto God's own promise, not simply believing a story is true. This trust alone makes us right with God, apart from our works. But faith never stands on nothing – it rests on the Word and the sacraments. At the altar, that promise is a testament: a gift left by someone about to die, which we simply receive and never offer back to God as a sacrifice.

We must be honest about one thing our own confession leaves genuinely open. It states, in one breath, that a person is accounted righteous and that a person is made righteous out of an unrighteous one. It does not itself say which wording rules the other; we do not settle that for you either.

Here is the article as our confession signed it before the Emperor:

We also teach that people cannot be justified before God by their own strength, merit, or work. They are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, when they believe they are received into favor and their sins are forgiven for Christ's sake. He, by His death, made satisfaction for our sins. God counts this faith as righteousness in His sight.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
We believed justification by faith alone because we held that no terrified conscience could ever rest on what it had done – only on what God had done. The old way left people endlessly uncertain, adding work to work, never knowing if they had done enough. We said instead: faith clings to something outside itself – the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution – and that trust alone is what makes a sinner right with God, for Christ's sake, apart from any strength or merit of ours. This was not license. Good works follow faith, uncommanded, the way fruit follows a living tree. But they follow it; they never buy it.

What convinced us was Scripture itself, heard again after lying, our founder said, forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under layers of teaching not its own. The Word did the work, not our own argument. And the cost was real: two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels in 1523 for refusing to take back what they had come to hold. That was not theory. That was the promise, held to its price.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
We hold one story that comes closest, though it is thin and we will not claim more for it than it can bear. Somewhere in Wittenberg, a wanderer down from Prussia is remembered to have sung Paul Speratus's own hymn beneath our founder's window – "Es ist das Heil uns kommen her," salvation has come to us – and the tradition says it moved him deeply. That hymn carries exactly what we have been speaking of: that salvation comes not by merit or by works, but by grace, through faith, for Christ's sake alone. But we must be honest. No vendored source says exactly when this happened, or names the singer, or confirms the scene ever happened at all. It reaches us as a remembered tradition, not as documented fact.

What we hold more firmly is this: years afterward, Johann Walter, our founder's own musical collaborator, remembered being kept at Wittenberg three weeks running while our founder worked out, tone by tone, how the Gospel and Epistle should be sung in German – and remembered, too, the poor charity-scholars going door to door singing for their bread, until the day the first German Mass was sung in the parish church. That is someone who lived it out: not a wanderer whose name we cannot give you, but a named musician who stayed three weeks to set the promise to a tune ordinary people could sing.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
That our own founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that it did not work. Not in one frustrated moment, but repeatedly, and not about strangers – about pastors and preachers of our own. In one parish he said flatly that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. Years later, writing for the whole territory, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent, and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly. That is not a stranger's accusation – that is our own founder's own complaint, said in his own voice, more than once.

We must be careful here, and honest about what we actually hold. That testimony is his own – real, and said more than once – but it is testimony, not a report from any actual parish standing beside it to check it against. We do not have the records that would tell us whether he was right about how bad it really was, only that he believed it and said so.

Even at his own table, the question was asked. Katharina asked why some prayed with such fervor under the old system while we, under the new one, prayed so coldly and carelessly. Our founder answered her plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent.

In March 1522, returned from the Wartburg, he preached eight days running to his own congregation, telling them to their faces that they had learned the words of the reform and not yet its love.

Here is what I want you to understand. We handed you a program – the household examined weekly, prayer three times a day, the three parts said for life. We can tell you exactly what it asked for. Whether any household kept it the way the book prescribed is a different question, and one our own record cannot answer from the inside. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. What we have instead is our founder's own persistent testimony that the Gospel was taught and not held – real, repeated, and never softened. That testimony is the hardest true thing about us, and we do not hide it.

sources.locus: 'an ass can almost intone the lessons... God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers' (v2 14676-14688); 'we see to our sorrow that many pastors and preachers are very negligent' (LC 51-52); Katharina von Bora's own question about coldness in prayer (TT 3147-3150)

Luther's own answer to the coldness question, verified verbatim there against cic/texts/luther_table-talk_bell1886.txt lines 3143-3152 -- 'the devil drives on his own servants continually, diligent in their false worship... but we, indeed, are ice cold therein, and negligent'

confidence.divergence_note: Documented as our founder's own testimony, given more than once across a decade; Contested at the scholarly level whether that testimony describes real congregations or is rhetoric, and this record carries witt.force.parishes-state-as-reported's own explicit bar forward: nothing here may be read as evidence that any actual Saxon congregation was in fact cold, ignorant, or negligent.

end_references.label: the household -- father, wife, children, servants; the catechism's own site
